More broadly, the empirical analysis of decentralized-oracle attack surfaces (Liu et al., 2022) applies: a single-mechanism oracle environment concentrates operational risk in one infrastructure, regardless of whether the mechanism itself is whitelisted or open. We return to this in the planned Paper 3 of this series.

The retained material on negRisk grouping below is unchanged: it is a mechanismindependent feature of Polymarket’s market structure. A related structural feature: Polymarket’s negRisk adapter resolves mutually-exclusive event groups at the group level rather than at the individual-market level. Individual-market outcomes within a negRisk group are derived from the group resolution. This paper treats negRisk-grouped markets at the group level where the data permits, and notes the derivation explicitly where individual-market outcome is required.

9.4 Framework boundaries The framework of Section 7 is specified for one instrument class: the Probability-Index Resolution-Aware Perpetual (PIRAP), a margin-collateralized perpetual on a single binary prediction-market event. We do not specify or evaluate frameworks for any of the following variants enumerated in plan v1.2 section 1: conditional-probability perpetuals, event-spread perpetuals, event-basket perpetuals, volatility perpetuals, liquidity-index perpetuals, rolling perpetuals, or funding-only structures. These are the subject of a companion paper (Paper 2 in our planned series) and are outside the scope of this work. The framework’s parameter discipline (Section 7.1) classifies every parameter as either estimated or policy-calibrated, but it does not specify a single optimal parameter setting. Different platform contexts may calibrate the policy parameters differently. The sensitivity analysis in Appendix E reports behavior across stated ranges; a particular numerical setting is a platform-specific choice. The framework specifies a listing eligibility decision rule (Section 7.10) that is binary at the quantitative tier (SEA ≥ SEA,min ) and flag-based at the governance tier. We do not develop a fine-grained or risk-tiered listing decision rule (e.g., differential maximum leverage by event class). Such refinements are platform-specific extensions on top of the framework as specified.

9.5 Scope of microstructure coverage The framework treats book depth as a first-class engine input: Dt enters the composite robust index (Section 7.2), the position-size margin add-on (Section 7.3), the liquidation-tranching procedure, and the resolution-zone protocol’s leverage-compression schedule. The empirical evaluation of E1 measures depth asymmetry (SF1) and the resolution-time depth collapse posited by Empirical Condition 1 (SF9). This is non-trivial microstructure coverage relative to typical risk-engine specifications, which treat liquidity as an exogenous parameter or omit it. That said, several microstructure dimensions are partially covered or out of scope, and naming them is the right intellectual honesty.

Liquidity time-dynamics beyond depth-collapse. Empirical Condition 1 formalizes one specific time-varying property of book liquidity: contraction in the final ∆R before resolution. We do not model other time-dynamic properties: depth volatility ∂Dt /∂t outside the resolution zone, depth persistence (the rate at which the book refills after a liquidity-consuming trade), or the relationship between depth and quote-update frequency (a thin book that updates fast carries different information than a thick book that updates slowly). The framework’s

parameters (Dtmin , ηtrnch ) are calibrated against snapshot depth, not against time-derived liquidity measures. Extending the framework to incorporate persistence and refresh-rate features is a natural follow-up.

Signed order flow and adverse-selection measurement. The PMXT v2 archive includes last_trade_price events with both side and transaction_hash, providing ground-truth signed order flow at the event level (Dubach, 2026). The framework’s adverse-selection discussion in Section 3.1 is conceptual; we do not estimate order-flow imbalance (OFI), Kyle’s λ, or realized-versus-effective-spread decomposition on the analysis sample. These are the measurement primitives that distinguish informed flow from noise, particularly in the resolution zone where the distinction matters most. We treat them as Paper 3 territory because their natural use-case is the manipulation and insider-risk analysis Paper 3 develops; their omission from Paper 1 is a scope choice, not an oversight.

For Paper 1’s PIRAP variant this is acceptable; multi-leg ELP variants (event-spread, event-basket) of Paper 2 will need explicit treatment. These scope statements are not apologies for omissions. 9.6 What the paper cannot establish Three classes of claim the paper does not address.

Real-world outcome manipulation. The framework analyzes manipulation of market price (via the index manipulation cost κt and the depth-aware liquidation rules); it does not analyze manipulation of the underlying event (e.g., bribing an athlete, leaking a policy decision, perpetrating an act intended to move an event market). Real-world outcome manipulation is a distinct problem with distinct incentives and is the subject of a companion paper (Paper 3 in our planned series). Statements in this paper about manipulation refer to market-price manipulation only.

Welfare across trader populations. The empirical evaluation in Section 8 reports survivability and continuity metrics on observed paths under counterfactual engine configurations. It does not report welfare distributions across distinct trader populations (retail vs. professional, informed vs. uninformed, hedger vs. speculator). The synthetic trader-population layer in E2c is a robustness layer, not a welfare-distribution model. A welfare analysis would require either real account-level data (unavailable) or a calibrated structural model (not specified).

Regulatory compliance. The paper makes no claim about the regulatory status of any particular implementation of an event-linked perpetual product in any specific jurisdiction. Existing regulatory frameworks for event contracts (CFTC in the US, jurisdictional analogues elsewhere) and for leveraged derivatives are distinct, evolving, and require legal expertise the authors do not claim. The pilot path in Section 10 explicitly defers jurisdiction-specific regulatory review to platforms that choose to adopt it.

9.7 Resolution-window structural ceiling A specific empirical limitation that emerged during the sample adequacy gate evaluation deserves documentation here because of its structural nature. Of the markets in the stratified analysis sample, 17.4% resolved within the 168-hour empirical window. The remaining 82.6% of markets either did not have a terminal state observed within the window (resolution scheduled after window end, or post-window cancellation) or had their early life truncated by the archive start boundary 2026-04-13T19 UTC. The chronological-prefix subsamples reported earlier (34.6% on 1K, 27.3% on 15K, with the 50K subsample revealing that nearly 80% of its markets had lifetimes exceeding the window itself) were day-1-biased per the finding in Section 5.5; the stratified figure is the reliable estimate. The stratified-sample ceiling is the structural ceiling on resolution-conditional analyses for the empirical week. Three specific implications:

1. Analyses that require the resolution outcome R ∈ {0, 1} are bounded by this ceiling. Proposition 1 evaluation (the static-margin shortfall proposition, which requires terminal collapse to be observed) is conducted only on resolved markets; Proposition 2 evaluation (the funding instability proposition, which does not require resolution and operates on the basis dynamics across the lifetime) uses the full sample. The two propositions therefore have different underlying n.

9.8 SF2 terminal-observation coverage The terminal-jump-magnitude test E1.2 (Section 8.1) is computed on the 77% of resolved analysis-sample markets with usable terminal observations: at least one price-change event in the final hour before resolution. The remaining 23% (3,061 of 13,298 analysis-sample markets, with 3,236 in the resume range specifically) had no observable price-change events in their final hour and therefore no |∆It [τ − 1h, τ ]| quantity to measure. The question is what this 23% represents:

• Genuine illiquidity in the final hour. Markets whose order books became inactive before resolution because the outcome was already near-certain and active market-making ceased. If this dominates, the 23% are markets where the engine’s index estimator must already be operating against a frozen book before the formal terminal jump arrives.

• Computation gap. Markets with observable activity in the final hour that the SF2 measurement logic missed, through a bug or data-pipeline gap. If this dominates, the 23% should be re-computable on a corrected logic.

The classification was completed on a 50-market random sanity sample (CC-006b, commit [SHA]). All 50 sampled markets show genuine illiquidity: zero observable price-change events, zero observable book updates in the final hour before resolution. The classification of the cohort is therefore "genuine illiquidity" and not "computation gap"; the markets in the 23% are markets whose order books were completely dark in the final hour before resolution. The framework implication is direct: an additional 3,236 of 13,298 markets (24%) had no displayed liquidity at all near resolution, beyond the structurally near-zero near-mid depth documented by SF9. This independently supports the refined Empirical Condition 1 characterization of near-mid depth as structurally absent: in 24% of the resolved analysis-sample markets, total displayed depth itself is empirically zero in the final hour, a fortiori case of the refined assumption.

Class composition of the illiquidity cohort. The 3,244 missing-SF2 markets distribute across event classes as: "other" 43%, sports 35%, crypto 13%, politics 9%. Comparing to the sample composition (sports ≈ 78% of three-class total, "other" ≈ remainder, crypto ≈ 11%, politics ≈ 9%), the "other" class is materially over-represented in the illiquidity cohort and sports is under-represented. Sports markets remain active through resolution, consistent with the SF8 finding that sports activity surges 2.5× in the final 24 hours; "other" class markets (long-tail event markets) go dark long before resolution. This class-conditional pattern is descriptive but it does not change the refined-assumption interpretation: the 24% are dark at resolution regardless of class, and the engine framework’s resolution-zone protocol operates without near-mid execution liquidity in the resolution window for any class.

The resume pass emitted per-market values for resume-coverage markets only. Per-class median, p25, and p75 statistics that would require pooling per-market values across both passes are therefore not reported in this revision. Pooled medians on each pass independently are available and are reported in Section 8.1 (E1.2), with cross-pass coincidence to four significant figures supporting the structural interpretation. A re-run of base aggregation with the resume-pass emission code would close this gap; this is deferred as a follow-up improvement and does not affect the E1.2 pass status.

9.9 Liquidity-measure refinement of Assumption 4 Empirical Condition 1 as stated in Section 6 is a post-failure diagnostic refinement, not a pre-registered structural assumption. We document the methodological event explicitly here because pre-registration discipline depends on visible accounting of prediction failures.

What was registered and what failed. Prior to running the empirical analysis, we registered a contraction prediction on total displayed depth within ±200 basis points of mid: median depth would contract toward resolution by some factor α ∈ (0, 1). SF9 measured the registered quantity directly. The result inverted the prediction. Median total displayed depth grew nearly fivefold between the [12h, 3h) and [3h, 1h) time-to-resolution buckets (8,940 USDC to 43,908 USDC at the median market). The contraction prediction failed on its registered measure.

What we did with the failure. We tested three hypotheses (H1: region-conditional contraction; H2: near-mid depth is empty throughout; H3: path-dependent contraction). H2 received the strongest support: with the depth window narrowed from ±200 to ±50 basis points, median depth is empirically zero throughout the market lifecycle and across all event classes. The Polymarket spread profile in SF4 supports this directly: median half-spreads at mid-region prices are 0.27 (27,000 basis points), so the ±50 basis point window almost never contains displayed quote size.

Diagnostic, not retroactive pre-registration. The near-mid depth finding is an empirical diagnostic that emerged from analyzing why the registered prediction failed. We do not present it as a post-hoc replacement for the failed prediction. The paper treats it as a refinement that informs interpretation of liquidation feasibility and as an input to the resolution-zone protocol design. The failure-mode propositions in Section 6 (Propositions 1–2) rest on Assumptions 1–3 only; Empirical Condition 1 is adjacent to but not premise of those propositions.

The liquidation-walking alternative. The diagnostic finding rests on an implicit assumption that warrants explicit discussion: the engine liquidates at the prevailing mid. An alternative engine design — one that walks the book through the deep out-of-the-money convergence-trade ladders, accepting the spread cost — could in principle execute liquidations even when near-mid depth is empty. The total displayed depth observed in SF9 within ±200 basis points of mid is non-trivial in the final hour (median 51,573 USDC at the analysis sample). Walking the book to access this depth is therefore not impossible; it is costly. The question is whether the cost is bounded enough that an engine could absorb it within its margin envelope, dispensing with the need for leverage compression. The empirical answer points toward the framework’s design. SF4 documents that effective half-spreads at mid-region prices are 0.27. At a leverage level L = 5, the maintenance margin buffer is approximately 0.20 of position notional. Walking the book through depth at progressively worse prices in the mid region means the realized execution price differs from the prevailing mid by at least the half-spread; for adverse moves of comparable magnitude on top, the realized loss approaches or exceeds the margin buffer in the median case at L = 5 and certainly at higher leverage. An engine willing to walk the book would therefore still face a shortfall on the median resolved market. This argues for leverage compression as an alternative to walking-book execution: the framework’s compression schedule reduces position size before the resolution zone, which (i) lowers the collateral requirement, and (ii) bounds the absolute cost of any walking-book execution that remains. A second consideration favoring leverage compression over walking-book execution is the manipulation channel. Walking the book through OTM convergence-trade ladders concentrates

execution against the market makers who placed those ladders. If a non-trivial fraction of those market makers are correlated with informed flow about the resolution outcome (Section 9.4), walking-book execution provides them a final-hour cross-trade against the engine’s liquidations. The resolution-zone protocol’s staged halt blocks this. We do not formalize a manipulation cost model in this paper (it is in scope for Paper 3); we note the qualitative point as additional motivation for the framework’s choice. E2b will provide a direct empirical test of this argument. The deterministic position grid evaluated under engine C0 (no compression) computes insurance-fund drawdown on observed paths, including any walking-book execution that C0 would have done. The drawdown comparison between C0 and C2 (full PIRAP with compression) tests whether walking the book preserved engine survival or displaced loss into the insurance fund. We report the comparison in Section 8.2.2 when E2 is complete.

9.10 Pre-emption trade-off in dynamic margin The framework’s jump-aware tiered margin (Definition 4) recomputes maintenance margin at each tick, with the continuous-vol component scaling with the running realized-volatility estimate σ̂t . This dynamic responsiveness is central to the framework’s intended behavior: as risk rises, required collateral rises; positions with insufficient collateral are liquidated before the situation deteriorates further. The empirical evaluation (Section 8.2) reveals a trade-off this design did not fully anticipate.

The empirical pattern. On observed Polymarket price paths, the dynamic-margin schedule pre-empts more liquidations than it prevents. When σ̂t rises in response to ordinary price noise — not yet a true terminal jump — the engine demands additional collateral; positions with limited margin buffer are liquidated. If the noise event passes without converting to a terminal jump, the position would have recovered under a static maintenance margin. Net effect across the analysis sample: the framework engine C2 liquidates more positions than the naive static-margin baseline C0, even though the framework is designed to protect against the larger-magnitude terminal-jump events. The framework’s directional improvements (insurance fund drawdown, median trader PnL) are real but smaller in magnitude than the pre-registered floors anticipated.

Why this is a fundamental design tension. Pre-emption of recoveries is the dual of pre-emption of true disasters. A margin schedule responsive enough to catch terminal jumps must also respond to noise events that look similar in their early phase. Distinguishing noise from imminent jump requires forward-looking information that the engine’s state-only inputs (realized volatility, current index, time to resolution) cannot provide. The design tension is not specific to our parameter choices; it is structural to dynamic-margin engines on bounded event-resolved underlyings.

Implications for design. Three responses to the pre-emption trade-off appear in the design space:

1. Hybrid margin schedule. Static margin throughout the pre-resolution period; dynamic activation only within ∆R of resolution. Avoids pre-emption on early-life noise while preserving terminal-jump protection when terminal jumps actually arrive. Untested in this paper; proposed for future work.

2. Halt-only evaluation variant. Resolution-zone halt protocol without continuous-margin reaction. Tests whether the halt component independently has value. Evaluated in E3 (Section 8.3).

3. Class-specific parameterization. The pre-emption cost varies by class (Section 8.2, perclass breakdown shows crypto class largest framework benefit, sports smallest). Selective deployment per class where the framework’s protection-versus-pre-emption balance is favorable.

This paper does not advocate full PIRAP deployment as specified. The framework as evaluated provides empirical characterization and directional improvement on welfare-side metrics; design recommendations for deployable variants follow in Section 10.

9.11 Halt-protocol scope: execution-channel risk vs. terminal-collapse risk The empirical evaluation in E3 (Section 8.3) makes explicit a scope distinction that was implicit in the framework specification: the resolution-zone halt protocol family (Definition 7) addresses execution-channel liquidation risk, but it does not address terminal-jump bad-debt risk. These risk channels are distinct, and they require distinct framework components. The halt protocol works as designed at the execution channel; terminal-jump risk lives in the margin schedule (Definition 4), not in the halt protocol.

The empirical pattern. On the analysis sample, the full multi-stage protocol M 3 reduces final-hour liquidation rate by 80.4% versus the naive M 0 baseline (Floor 1 PASS). The reduction is real but mechanically explained: the staged trading halt at τ − ∆R closes the venue before in-flight liquidations can occur in the final window. The reduction is therefore not evidence that the halt protocol prevents losses — it is evidence that the halt protocol prevents one specific channel of loss (in-flight liquidation under deteriorating margin during the final hour) which is itself rare under M 0 (∼ 0.1% of position triples). The framework’s halt protocol does not affect terminal-jump bad-debt frequency, which is essentially identical under M 3 (+2.4%, slightly worse) and M 0. The M 3 slightly-worse result is explained by the small cost of foregoing favorable intra-window moves under the halt: positions forced to close at the prevailing index price at τ − ∆R miss the small fraction of paths that would have moved favorably between halt and resolution.

Why this is a scope finding, not a calibration finding. The bad-debt frequency of approximately 54% pooled under M 0 is structurally predicted from SF2: median terminal jump is |∆It | = 0.50 percentage points while the maintenance margin buffer at L = 5 is approximately 0.20 percentage points. In approximately half of resolved markets, a leveraged long position structurally cannot cover the terminal-collapse loss with its own collateral. No halt-timing choice can eliminate this loss, because the loss is realized at oracle settlement, not during the halt window. The structural prediction follows from Assumption 1 and Proposition 1 taken together: if the underlying collapses to one of two fixed endpoints from a mid-region pre-collapse price, and the maintenance margin buffer is a fraction of position notional, then for any |∆It | exceeding the maintenance fraction the position cannot cover the loss. Halt timing affects when settlement occurs relative to the trading venue’s last activity; it does not affect the collateral sufficiency of the position at settlement.

We document this scope finding here rather than retroactively rewriting Section 7; the framework’s component definitions stand as proposed, and the scope distinction is one of the design lessons of the paper rather than a correction to the framework’s specification.

9.12 Empirical limitations The empirical evaluation in Section 8 is constrained in several ways that bear on interpretation. First, the analysis sample is sports-dominant (77.9% of three-class total), so primary crossclass claims are sports-anchored; politics and crypto findings are reported but the underrepresentation limits generalizability of class-conditional claims. Second, the resolution-window structural ceiling of 17.4% (Section 9.7) bounds the number of markets on which terminal-state analyses (E1.2, E2 resolution-zone metrics, E3) can be computed; the resulting test set sizes per class — particularly politics, where the number of resolved markets within the empirical window is smallest — limit statistical power on per-class falsifiability tests beyond E1.1 and E1.2. Third, several of the descriptive findings revealed class-level dispersion (SF8 resolution-time activity surge ranging from 0.68× in politics to 24.6× in crypto; SF6 trade size distributions varying ≈ 9× in mean across classes) that suggests a single-engine-parameterization assumption is too strong; the framework’s class-aware parameter design (documented in Definition 7 and Section C.3) accommodates this but the empirical parameterization itself is a research item beyond this paper’s scope.

10 Future Research Agenda The empirical evaluation of Section 8 establishes whether the resolution-aware framework behaves coherently on observed Polymarket paths within a specific window. It does not establish that the findings generalize, that the framework is robust against adversarial conditions not present in the observed sample, or that the listing eligibility framework is appropriate outside the data the paper examines. Each of these is a research question; this section identifies them and the research extensions that would address them. We list the extensions in order of increasing distance from the present paper’s evidence base. We do not specify decision rules, thresholds, or implementation details: those would prejudge the research design of work that has not yet been done. The intent is to make explicit what the present paper does not establish and what follow-up research would be needed to establish it.

10.1 Adversarial replay extensions The counterfactual replay in E2 evaluates engine configurations on observed price paths. Observed paths reflect whatever adversarial or manipulative behavior was already present in the Polymarket sample, but they do not test the framework against engineered adversarial scenarios that did not occur in the sample.

Examples of scenarios that would be informative: coordinated spoofing of one or more index components designed to shift It without moving the underlying market price; late-resolution information injection at varying time-to-resolution distances; oracle-dispute escalation under different proposer-whitelist configurations; cross-market correlation shocks affecting baskets of related markets simultaneously. A natural design is deterministic modification of observed paths to inject the adversarial scenario, with the modification’s parameters varied across a documented sensitivity range. The present paper does not include this extension because the formal specification of adversarial scenarios is itself a research question that interacts with the manipulation analysis deferred to Paper 3.

10.2 Cross-platform replication Findings in this paper are Polymarket-specific within the v2 archive window (see Section 9.2). The framework specification of Section 7 is platform-agnostic by construction — its inputs are observable microstructure features — but the empirical findings are not. The natural replication target is Kalshi, the largest CFTC-regulated event-contract venue with a CLOB structure comparable to Polymarket but with different regulatory frame, collateral asset, and trader population. Other CLOB-based event venues with sufficient public data could also serve. Replication would not be a port of the framework; it would be a re-execution of the same framework on a different observed dataset. We do not undertake cross-platform replication in this paper because public-data access for Kalshi at PMXT-comparable granularity is, at the time of writing, less mature than for Polymarket. Replication becomes feasible as comparable data becomes available.

10.3 Live observability without leverage A research extension that does not involve leverage at all is to implement the engine’s index, margin, funding, and liquidation rules as a real-time observable computation against live Polymarket data, without ever extending leverage to any participant. The output of this implementation is a public time series of what the engine would have done; the absence of capital at risk avoids the deployment question entirely. The research interest of this extension is twofold: it provides a real-time stress test against data that was not in the empirical window, and it produces a public artifact that other researchers could use to validate the framework’s behavior independently. This extension is research, not deployment; we mention it here as one specific way to extend the empirical evidence base without invoking any of the questions about leverage extension that the paper deliberately leaves unanswered (Section 9.6).

10.4 Boundaries we do not address Three classes of follow-up work are outside this paper’s scope and outside the scope of the extensions above. First, the question of whether any deployable product based on the framework would be appropriate in any specific jurisdiction is a regulatory and legal question, not a research question we are positioned to address. Regulatory frameworks for event contracts and for leveraged derivatives differ materially across jurisdictions and continue to evolve. Independent legal review would be a precondition for any deployment-related research, and that review is outside the scope of academic empirical work. Second, the welfare-distribution question — how engine configurations interact with different trader populations, what fraction of trader losses concentrate in identifiable informationasymmetry classes, and whether the framework reduces or amplifies retail-versus-professional

outcome divergence — requires either real account-level data or a calibrated structural model. Neither is available within the present empirical setup. A welfare analysis would extend the present work substantially and is the subject of Paper 3 in our planned series, where the manipulation and trader-asymmetry analyses also live. Third, the question of whether the specific instrument analyzed (PIRAP) is the right entry point into the broader event-linked perpetual design space, versus a conditional-probability or event-spread or volatility variant, is the subject of Paper 2 in our planned series. Paper 2 develops the taxonomy systematically; Paper 1’s evaluation of PIRAP is one entry in the taxonomy. These three boundaries are not weaknesses of the present paper; they are scope statements. A reader interested in any of them should expect to find them addressed in the companion papers, with the empirical backbone of Paper 1 as a prerequisite.

10.5 Design recommendations from the empirical findings The empirical evaluation surfaced specific design tensions that inform deployable variants of the framework. We collect concrete recommendations here. Each recommendation is grounded in a specific empirical finding from Section 5.6 or Section 8; we cite the finding alongside the recommendation.

Recommendation 1: Hybrid margin schedule. The dynamic margin pre-emption trade-off documented in Section 9.10 suggests a structural alternative to PIRAP’s continuousdynamic margin: hold static maintenance margin throughout the pre-resolution period, and activate dynamic margin only within ∆R of resolution. This avoids pre-emption on early-life price noise (the dominant source of liquidations on observed paths in the analysis sample) while preserving terminal-jump protection in the resolution zone (where SF2’s median |∆It | = 0.5 confirms the design need is real). The hybrid variant has not been evaluated empirically in this paper; it is a design recommendation with testable structure.

Recommendation 2: Halt-only evaluation variant. The resolution-zone halt protocol (Definition 7) is separable from the dynamic-margin schedule. A configuration that pairs static margin with the multi-stage halt — without continuous dynamic-margin reaction — isolates the execution-channel value of the staged halt without inducing the pre-emption trade-off documented in Section 9.10. It does not address the terminal-jump bad-debt channel identified in Proposition 1; that channel remains margin-side, and a halt-only configuration leaves it unaddressed. The relative execution-channel contribution of the halt component is the empirical content of E3 (Section 8.3); whether this variant is a useful starting point for further evaluation work, with the bad-debt channel addressed separately by margin-side mechanisms, follows from those results. We do not propose this configuration as a deployable specification; the broader scope statement of Section 1.6 applies.

Recommendation 3: Class-specific parameterization. The class dispersion documented in SF6 (trade size; politics median 20 USDC vs. crypto median 10), SF7 (time-of-day patterns; sports peaks 17–21 UTC vs. crypto/politics 14–15 UTC), and SF8 (resolution-time activity surge; crypto 24.6× vs. politics 0.68×) implies that a single set of engine parameters is illsuited across event classes. Production deployments should calibrate margin coefficients (mσ , mJ ), resolution-zone window ∆R , and leverage caps Lmax (t) per event class. The per-class drawdown findings in E2b (where crypto class shows the largest framework benefit and sports the smallest) provide quantitative anchoring for class-specific calibration.

Recommendation 4: Realistic baseline calibration for production evaluation. The pre-registered E2 evaluation (Section 8.2) compared the framework to a naive crypto-perp port baseline (C0) with mσ = 1.0 calibration. Production evaluations should evaluate against whichever margin schedule is actually deployed elsewhere; if the realistic baseline differs from C0, the comparative metrics will differ accordingly. Paper 1’s E0 baseline is a research benchmark, not a production-equivalent margin engine.

Recommendation 5: Position-size assumptions should match observed trader populations. The deterministic position grid in E2b (100, 1000, 10000 USDC notional) substantially exceeds the observed Polymarket trade-size distribution from SF6 (medians 10–20 USDC across classes). Production evaluations of any event-linked engine should match the realistic trader population: small positions per the SF6 distribution rather than fixed grids. The framework’s drawdown metrics on realistic position sizes will differ from the E2b values, in ways that depend on the realistic distribution.

Limits of these recommendations. None of the five recommendations is empirically validated in this paper. They are design directions that follow from the empirical findings. Each would require its own empirical evaluation under appropriate discipline (pre-registered floors, transparent reporting of results, honest acknowledgment of failures) before deployment claims can be made. The hybrid margin design (Recommendation 1) is the most concrete; we identify it as the natural follow-up empirical question.

11 Conclusion The empirical evaluation of Section 8 produces a clear and complex picture. Of five preregistered materiality floors, three fail in magnitude (E2a liquidation rate, E2b drawdown reduction, E3 Floor 2 bad-debt frequency) and two pass (E2c median welfare direction, E3 Floor 1 final-hour liquidation rate). Of the two passes, E3 Floor 1’s 80.4% reduction reflects the mechanical effect of the staged trading halt rather than independent risk-discipline contribution. The framework as specified does not achieve the order-of-magnitude liquidation-rate or baddebt reduction we hypothesized at pre-registration. It does provide directional improvement on welfare-side metrics in the crypto class (−11.1% drawdown), modest improvement pooled across classes (−5.1% drawdown, +14% median trader PnL), and within-threshold welfare cost (−1.7% trader PnL under R3 vs R0). Two design lessons emerge from the empirical evidence. First, the resolution-zone halt protocol family addresses execution-channel liquidation risk but does not address terminaljump bad-debt risk — terminal-jump risk lives in the margin schedule, not the halt protocol, and these are distinct framework components requiring distinct design treatment. Second, dynamic-margin reaction pre-empts more recoveries than it prevents on observed paths: a structural trade-off between protection against terminal-collapse scenarios and protection of ordinary recoveries, replicated across two independent counterfactual replays (E2 and E3). The pre-emption trade-off is not a parameter calibration artifact; it is a fundamental property of dynamic-margin engines on bounded event-resolved underlyings. Sports-class evidence is primary per the sports-dominance consequence rule (Section 5.5); politics and crypto are reported as secondary classes that document framework behavior on classes other than the dominant one.

11.1 What this paper claims The paper delivers the seven outputs stated in Section 1.4; the central framework-performance claim (contribution 3) is qualified by the failed materiality floors as documented in Section 8.5,

and we restate each contribution below at the level of empirical support the evidence warrants. Empirical microstructure characterization (contribution 1) is empirically supported. SF1–SF9 on the analysis sample (13,298 usable markets passing adequacy gates, of which 13,115 resolved within the empirical window for E3 evaluation; locked-seed stratified-by-day selection from 61,087 ingested per Section 5.5) characterize the binary-event price process at the granularity required for derivative design. The depth-asymmetry property and terminal-jump magnitude pass their pre-registered floors with substantial margin. Two formal non-portability propositions (contribution 2) stand as proved. Propositions 1 and 2 rest on Assumptions 1 to 3 and do not depend on E2/E3 outcome. The propositions establish that naive transplant of crypto-perp mechanics fails on bounded prediction-market underlyings; this is a structural finding independent of the framework’s empirical performance against the naive baseline. Resolution-aware risk-engine framework (contribution 3) is characterized empirically with documented design tensions. The framework as specified does not achieve order-ofmagnitude liquidation-rate or bad-debt reduction relative to the naive baseline. It provides directional welfare-side improvement, with the largest benefit in the crypto class. Two design lessons (halt-vs-margin scope distinction; pre-emption trade-off) are now empirically anchored. Three-mode replay-based counterfactual back-test (contribution 4) is methodologically as specified. The trader-independent modes (E2a, E2b) controlling the central empirical claims operate without trader-population assumptions. E2c provides robustness under heterogeneous-trader aggregation. Two-tier listing eligibility framework (contribution 5) is specified but not empirically tested. The quantitative suitability score SEA and governance overlay BE are deploymentreadiness components for which empirical evaluation requires either prospective deployment data or simulated deployment records, neither of which is in scope for this paper. Reproducibility infrastructure (contribution 6) is delivered. The PMXT v2 archive ingest pipeline, sample-selection module with locked seed, run-loop with mid-stage stop conditions, round-robin queue ordering, persistent HTTP connections, SHA manifests, and endto-end reproduction script (Section D) constitute reusable public infrastructure for systematic Polymarket microstructure research. Future research agenda (contribution 7) and the five deployment-direction recommendations of Section 10.5 translate the empirical findings into specific testable design refinements: hybrid margin schedule, halt-only evaluation variant, class-specific parameterization, realistic baseline calibration for production evaluation, and realistic position-size assumptions matching observed trader populations. The paper delivers seven outputs; the central framework-performance claim is qualified by the failed materiality floors. The empirical evaluation’s negative results are documented honestly as part of the contribution rather than as obstacles to overcome before the contribution is realized.

11.2 What this paper does not claim We restate, in concluding form, the boundaries already stated in Section 1.6 and Section 9. The paper does not propose a deployable product. It develops and evaluates a risk-engine framework on observed Polymarket paths under counterfactual replay; it does not establish that any implementation of that framework is appropriate for live deployment in any jurisdiction. The paper does not claim balanced cross-class evidence. The pre-registered Sample Adequacy Gate fired the sports-dominance consequence rule (Section 5.5); cross-class generalization claims are explicitly weakened where they would otherwise rest on under-represented classes. The paper does not claim findings transfer beyond Polymarket without replication. The framework is platform-agnostic by construction; the empirical findings are not. Cross-platform replication is identified as a research extension in Section 10.2, not undertaken here.

The paper does not develop a formal model of real-world outcome manipulation. The composite robust index of Section 7.2 and the governance overlay of Section 7.9 address marketprice manipulation as a design criterion; real-world outcome manipulation is the subject of a planned companion paper. The paper does not provide a cross-jurisdictional regulatory analysis. The pilot path of Section 10 explicitly defers jurisdiction-specific regulatory review to platforms that choose to adopt the framework. The paper does not present a welfare model across trader populations. Section 8 reports survivability and continuity metrics on observed paths; trader-welfare distribution analysis would require either real account-level data (unavailable) or a calibrated structural model (not specified). A reader who carries away from this paper the conclusion that “event-linked perpetuals are safe to deploy” has misread it. A reader who carries away “event-linked perpetuals are designed problems with measurable failure modes that admit measurable fixes, and the empirical evidence base for the proposed fixes can be extended through documented research extensions” has read it correctly.

11.3 Companion papers and research agenda This paper is the first of four planned papers on event-linked perpetuals and the microstructure of leveraged prediction-market venues. The structure of the series:

Paper 2: Taxonomy of event-linked perpetuals. Develops a formal taxonomy of the broader instrument class beyond PIRAP. Includes conditional-probability variants (per- (A) (B) petuals on P(A|B)), event-spread variants (perpetuals on pt − pt for related events), event-basket variants (perpetuals on weighted combinations of multiple event probabilities), volatility variants (perpetuals on Var(pt ) rather than pt itself), liquidity-index variants (perpetuals settling on depth or spread metrics), rolling variants (continuous succession of contracts on rolling event windows), and funding-only variants (no settlement; only funding flow). Each variant inherits the bounded-support and oracle-mediated resolution constraints documented in Paper 1, and each requires its own engine adaptations. Paper 2 specifies each variant, analyzes its design constraints relative to PIRAP, and characterizes empirical evaluability. What Paper 2 takes from Paper 1: the bounded-event process model (Section 3), the structural price-process properties of Section 3.1, the non-portability propositions of Section 6, and the framework components of Section 7. What Paper 2 adds: multi-leg and basket microstructure (cross-market liquidity coupling, conditional-probability oracle composition), variant-specific funding rules, and evaluability criteria for designs that may lack single-market analogs.

Paper 3: Manipulation, insider information, and regulation. Addresses manipulation theory and regulatory dimensions excluded from Paper 1. Three strands:

1. Manipulation incentive model (theoretical). Distinguishes market-price manipulation (scope of Paper 1’s index design) from real-world outcome manipulation (athletes throwing matches, voters being bribed, referee compromises, debate moderators behaving strategically). Models leverage as an amplifier of outcome-manipulation incentives and characterizes conditions under which leverage available on Polymarketclass venues materially shifts the cost-benefit calculus of real-world manipulation. 2. Insider-information exposure. Builds on ForesightFlow’s existing informed-flow detection framework (Information Leakage Score, Signal Credibility Index, per-market leakage analyses) rather than re-deriving informed-flow methodology. Paper 3’s

contribution in this strand is the leverage extension: how does leverage availability amplify insider information rents, and how does Paper 1’s pre-emption finding (Section 9.10) interact with this amplification. 3. Regulatory analysis. Cross-jurisdictional review of event-contract leverage status under CFTC, SFC (UK), MAS (Singapore), MiCA (EU), and other major frameworks; analysis of regulatory arbitrage paths between offshore CLOB venues, regulated CFTC exchanges (e.g., Kalshi), and decentralized deployments; and recommendations for a coherent regulatory taxonomy distinguishing gambling regulation from financial-contract regulation.

What Paper 3 takes from Paper 1: the design framework, the empirical microstructure characterization, the oracle-mechanism finding from Section 9.3, the pre-emption-tradeoff finding from Section 9.10, and the explicit scope statements of Sections 1.6 and 9. What Paper 3 adds: the manipulation theory and regulatory analysis that Paper 1 deliberately leaves to be developed on the empirical foundation Paper 1 establishes.

Paper 4: Non-retail liquidity provision and microstructure on Polymarket. Empirical characterization of non-retail Polymarket participants — market makers, arbitrageurs, liquidity providers, whales — using PMXT v2 transaction-level data (transaction_hash, side, size, timestamp). Pseudonymous addresses are clustered by behavioral signatures (quote intensity, directional bias, holding period, two-sided ratio, cross-market activity); per-cluster microstructure characterization follows. Paper 4 complements ForesightFlow’s existing demand-side informed-flow analyses by providing the supply-side counterpart: who provides liquidity, and how does that supply behave near resolution and around information events. What Paper 4 takes from Paper 1: the empirical microstructure characterization (Section 5.6), the refined liquidity diagnostic of Empirical Condition 1, the per-class dispersion documented in SF6 and SF8, and the PMXT v2 infrastructure. What Paper 4 adds: pertrader behavioral feature engineering, behavioral clustering of pseudonymous addresses, per-cluster microstructure analysis, negRisk arbitrage flow analysis, and supply-side manipulation patterns (spoof, wash, coordinated quote withdrawal) complementary to Paper 3’s demand-side incentive analysis.

A reader interested in any of the boundaries Paper 1 declares should expect to find them addressed in Papers 2, 3, and 4, with Paper 1’s empirical backbone and framework specification as a prerequisite. The four papers are intended to be readable as a coherent series: each paper’s contributions are sharper because the others’ contents exist. Together with the ForesightFlow papers cited in Papers 3 and 4 (Nechepurenko, 2026a,b,d,g), the programme provides substantively complete research coverage of leveraged prediction-market venues from microstructure, mechanism design, and policy perspectives.

11.4 Open questions The empirical findings raise specific open questions, organized by which of the future research extensions of Section 10 could address them.

Addressable through hybrid-margin empirical evaluation (Section 10.5 Recommendation 1). Does a margin schedule that decouples pre-resolution dynamics from resolutionzone dynamics escape the pre-emption trade-off documented in E2a and E3 M 1/M 2? The hypothesis that static margin throughout the pre-resolution period combined with dynamic activation only within ∆R of resolution preserves terminal-jump protection while avoiding pre-emption is testable on the same PMXT v2 archive infrastructure delivered with this paper.

Addressable through halt-only empirical evaluation (Section 10.5 Recommendation 2). Does deploying the staged-halt protocol of Definition 7 without the dynamic-margin reaction of Definition 4 preserve the Floor 1 mechanical reduction in final-hour liquidations while matching C0’s welfare? The CC-008 R3 mechanic provides the partial answer (−1.7% welfare cost vs C0); a direct halt-only-vs-naive comparison would isolate the halt contribution from the leverage-compression and dynamic-margin contributions.

Addressable through cross-platform replication (Section 10.2). Do the empirical findings transfer to other CLOB-based event venues with different oracle, collateral, and trader-population characteristics? The framework is platform-agnostic by construction; the finding that 3 of 5 floors fail in magnitude is platform-specific until replicated. Kalshi is the natural replication target.

Addressable through adversarial replay (Section 10.1). Do the floor-failure findings strengthen or weaken under engineered adversarial scenarios not present in the observed sample? The pre-emption trade-off is documented on natural-sample paths; whether targeted manipulation could exploit pre-emption to engineer cascade liquidations is the adversarial-replay question.

Outside the four research extensions: terminal-jump risk reduction. The bad-debt frequency finding (E3 Floor 2 fail) is structural: terminal-jump magnitude exceeds maintenance margin buffer at typical leverage levels. Reducing bad-debt frequency materially requires either (i) lower leverage caps, which is the Lmax (t) → 1 corner of Proposition 1 and defeats the purpose of leveraged event-linked perpetuals; or (ii) higher initial margin, which is feasible but reduces capital efficiency proportionally. The framework’s halt protocol is the wrong design lever for this risk, as documented; the right lever is the margin schedule, with the design tension that more aggressive margin worsens the pre-emption trade-off. Reconciling these tensions is the central design question for any deployable follow-up framework.

A Variable Glossary and Terminology This appendix collects every variable, parameter, and technical term introduced in the paper. The reader can use it as a reference while reading the body. The notation is the same as in the paper sections; this appendix introduces no parallel notation. Where a term has a corresponding cross-reference to a definition, proposition, or section, that reference is given.

A.1 Price processes pt Reference event-market price. The Polymarket outcome-token price observed at time t on the venue’s CLOB. Domain: [0, 1]. The reference price is the underlying that the event-linked perpetual contract settles against. (Section 3.1)

It Engine index price. The composite robust index used by the risk engine for margining, liquidation, and funding. A function of pt , depth, and three component estimators. (Definition 3)

qt Mark price. The perpetual-contract trading price observed on the engine’s order book, distinct from the index price. The basis is qt − It . (Section 3.1)

R Resolution outcome. The terminal value of the underlying event, R ∈ {0, 1}, observed at τ from the oracle.

A.2 Time variables τ Scheduled resolution time. The pre-announced time at which the underlying event is expected to resolve and the oracle to publish the outcome.

T Margin horizon end-point. A target time used in margin computations. In current usage, T is set equal to the current resolution time relative to which the margin schedule is computed.

(T − t) Time to resolution. The remaining time until scheduled resolution: T − t.

∆R Resolution-zone horizon. The window before τ within which the leverage compression and depth-collapse assumption (Empirical Condition 1) apply.

A.3 Engine state and margin Mtinit Initial margin requirement at time t. Total margin required to open a position of given notional. Decomposed into a continuous-volatility component and a jump-aware tiered component. (Definition 4)

Mtmaint Maintenance margin requirement at time t. The margin level below which a position is liquidated. Set as a fraction β < 1 of Mtinit .

Lmax (t) Maximum allowed leverage at time t. Time-dependent under the leverage compression schedule: Lmax (t)((T − t)) → 1 as (T − t) → 0. (Definition 5)

Ft Funding rate at time t. Periodic payment between long and short positions. Standard basis-only: Ft = c · (qt − It ). Boundary-corrected variant adds a regime-dependent term near It → 0 and It → 1. (Definition 6)

Λt Liquidation price. The reference-price level at which an open position triggers liquidation under the engine’s rules.

A.4 Microstructure observables Dt Within-200bps depth at time t. Total displayed quote size on either side of the prevailing mid-price within ±200 basis points. The default liquidity primitive used throughout the paper. (Section 3.1)

Dtmin Thinness threshold. The depth level below which the engine biases the index toward 0.5 by a small amount εthin .

ρ Boundary depth-asymmetry ratio. The ratio of depth on the structurally-thicker side of the boundary region to the thinner side. Pre-registered floor: ρ ≥ 1.5 at the median market. (Assumption 3)

α Resolution-time depth contraction factor. The factor by which displayed depth contracts in the final ∆R before resolution. α < 1 under Empirical Condition 1.

A.5 Risk and information observables π̂tjump Engine estimator of jump probability. Estimator of the probability of a terminal jump in It within the current margin horizon, conditional on observable proxies for information arrival. (Section 3.1, Section C)

σ̂t Windowed continuous-volatility estimator. Used in the continuous component of margin. Computed from windowed realized index variance.

κt Manipulation cost proxy. Notional cost to move the index It by a target ∆manip under a one-shot market-order execution model. A conservative book-thinness proxy, not an estimated impact coefficient. (Section C)

ρt Resolution-text clarity proxy. A scalar feature used by the governance overlay BE as an indicator of resolution-text ambiguity. Sourced from observable signals in the market metadata.

A.6 Open interest and listing OIt Open interest at time t. Total notional of open positions, both long and short. A function of position sizes summed across active accounts.

SEA Quantitative suitability score. First-tier listing eligibility score, computed deterministically from observable market features per Definition 8.

BE Governance overlay flag. Second-tier listing-eligibility input, capturing qualitative integrity concerns (resolution-text ambiguity, oracle dispute history, cross-market manipulation flags) per Definition 9.

A.7 Engine configurations C0 Naive crypto-perp port. Continuous-vol static margin, basis-only funding, no leverage compression, no resolution-zone protocol. The configuration whose structural failure modes are characterized in Propositions 1 and 2.

C1 Intermediate engine. Jump-aware tiered margin and leverage compression, but basis-only funding (no boundary correction) and no resolution-zone protocol.

C2 Full PIRAP engine. Composite robust index, jump-aware tiered margin, leverage compression schedule, boundary-corrected funding, and multi-stage resolution-zone protocol M 3.

A.8 Resolution-zone mechanics M 0 Naive forced expiry. Positions held through resolution; terminal collapse settles at oracle outcome.

M 1 Leverage compression only. Lmax (t)((T − t)) ramps to 1 as (T − t) → 0 per Definition 5; no boundary funding correction or staged halt.

M 2 Compression + boundary funding. Leverage compression plus boundary-corrected funding.

M 3 Full multi-stage protocol. Compression plus boundary funding plus staged-halt protocol with circuit-breaker fallback. (Section 7.7)

A.9 Experiments E1 Empirical characterization. Tests two pre-registered stylized facts on the analysis sample: depth asymmetry ρ ≥ 1.5 (E1.1) and median terminal jump magnitude ≥ 0.10 (E1.2). Evaluates SF1–SF9. (Section 8.1)

E2 Counterfactual replay. Three modes: position-agnostic survivability (E2a, trader-independent), deterministic position grid (E2b, trader-independent), synthetic-trader robustness layer (E2c). (Section 8.2)

E3 Resolution-zone stress test. Compares M 0, M 1, M 2, M 3 on resolved markets. Preregistered floors: ≥50% reduction in final-hour liquidations and ≥75% reduction in bad-debt events under M 3 versus M 0. (Section 8.3)

A.11 Acronyms and platform terms CLOB Central limit order book. The Polymarket trading venue is a CLOB (as opposed to an LMSR-based market maker).

ELP Event-linked perpetual. The class of derivative instruments analyzed in this paper. Paper 1 develops the PIRAP variant; Paper 2 develops the broader taxonomy.

PIRAP Probability-Indexed Resolution-Aware Perpetual. The specific event-linked perpetual variant whose risk engine is specified and evaluated in this paper.

OOv2 UMA Optimistic Oracle V2. The legacy resolution oracle on Polygon, used for longhorizon Polymarket markets created before the August 2025 governance migration.

MOOV2 Managed Optimistic Oracle V2. The current resolution oracle, with proposers restricted to a managed whitelist. Operational for new short-horizon markets and dominant in the empirical sample.

PMXT v2 Polymarket’s tick-level event-stream archive, version 2. Hourly Parquet partitions; primary source for the empirical work in this paper.

negRisk Polymarket’s adapter for mutually-exclusive event groups. Resolves at the group level rather than the individual-market level.

Gamma API Polymarket’s REST API for market metadata and outcome-price data. Endpoint: gamma-api.polymarket.com.

Goldsky Subgraph indexing service used for UMA OOv2 record access. Polygon-indexed.

B Data Schema and Ingestion Architecture The empirical work integrates four data components, all public: the PMXT v2 hourly archive (primary backbone), Polymarket Gamma API (market metadata), UMA Optimistic Oracle records on Polygon (resolution outcomes), and a news-window labels dataset (scheduled event indicators for the jump probability estimator). This appendix describes the schema of each and the join logic that combines them. The detailed schema tables below are populated for r2_post_g5; the present version provides the architectural overview.

B.1 PMXT v2 hourly archive The primary archive is a series of hourly-partitioned Parquet files containing the complete tick stream of Polymarket CLOB events. Each file covers exactly one UTC hour and contains every event of the four types listed below for every market with activity in that hour.

Event types. Four event types appear in the schema: book (full order-book snapshot), price_change (incremental order-book update), last_trade_price (executed trade), and tick_size_change (rare; tick-size configuration change).

Trade tape availability. Trade-level data is included in the primary archive via last_trade_price events. No separate trade-tape source is needed. (An earlier version of our data architecture postulated a separate trade-tape augmentation; the CC-001 ingestion module verified this is unnecessary.)

Schema columns (high-level). Sixteen columns; full table populated in r2_post_g5. Key fields used in this paper: timestamp_received (server ingestion time, primary sort key), timestamp (event authoring time, used for latency diagnostics), event_type, market (condition_id), asset_id (CLOB token, joins to Gamma clobTokenIds), and event-typespecific payload fields.

Access endpoint. Direct R2 enumeration: https://r2v2.pmxt.dev/polymarket_orderbook_<YYYY-MM-DD See Section 5.3 for why this is the canonical access pattern (and why the HTML index at archive.pmxt.dev is not).

B.2 Reconstructing the order book from PMXT events The book event provides a full snapshot; subsequent price_change events provide incremental updates. To reconstruct the order book at any timestamp, the procedure is:

1. Take the most recent book snapshot at or before the target timestamp.

2. Apply every price_change between that snapshot and the target timestamp in timestamp_received order.

3. Result: the order book as the venue knew it at the target timestamp.

A sanity-check spot test of this procedure on five markets is part of the G5 sample adequacy gate (Section 5.4); reconstructed best bid/ask must agree with feed best-bid/best-ask fields on at least 99% of price_change events.

B.3 Polymarket Gamma API: market metadata Public REST API at gamma-api.polymarket.com. Endpoints: /markets (per-market metadata) and /events (event groupings, used for tag enrichment).

Fields used. Market title, tags, outcomePrices (used for MOOV2 resolution detection; see Section B.4), clobTokenIds (joins to PMXT asset_id by exact ASCII string match), scheduled resolution date, resolution status.

B.4 UMA Optimistic Oracle: resolution metadata Two adapter mechanisms are active in the empirical window:

OOv2 (Optimistic Oracle V2). Standard UMA optimistic oracle. Records accessed via Goldsky-hosted subgraph indexing Polygon. Provides outcome (R ∈ {0, 1}), proposer address, disputer address (if any), and dispute timestamps.

MOOV2 (Managed Optimistic Oracle V2). Introduced under UMIP-189 in August 2025; restricts proposers to a managed whitelist. MOOV2 records are not in the standard Goldsky subgraph and are accessed instead via Polymarket’s Gamma API outcomePrices field (when the field reads as a deterministic 0/1 vector after finalization).

Adapter registry lock. Both adapters are registered in ingest/uma_resolutions.py at ADAPTER_REGISTRY_VERSION = 2026-05-05. The known address sets are KNOWN_OOV2_ADAPTERS and KNOWN_MOOV2_ADAPTERS. A new adapter address (e.g., from a future governance migration) requires registry update with version bump.

Implications for analysis. The two mechanisms have structurally different dispute-frequency baselines because of the proposer-whitelisting design difference. See Section 9.3 for the implications for cross-class comparisons.

B.5 News-window labels A labelled schedule of scheduled events (sports key moments, political debates, macro release timestamps) used as inputs to the π̂tjump jump-probability estimator (Section C). The specific source dataset is documented at the time it is used; for the empirical week 2026-04-21 to 2026-04-27, the schedule is hand-curated and committed to the repository for reproducibility.

B.6 PMXT-to-Gamma-to-UMA join logic The full join pipeline:

1. PMXT events are ingested by asset_id.

2. Gamma metadata is fetched for the unique asset_id set in the empirical window. Join is by exact-string match asset_id = clobTokenIds[i] for some outcome index i.

3. For each Gamma-resolved market, UMA OO records are fetched. OOv2 adapters are queried via Goldsky; MOOV2 adapters are queried via Gamma outcomePrices.

4. The combined record is persisted with the asset_id as primary key and oracle_source field tagging which adapter produced the resolution.

B.7 Cleaning steps 1. Sort all events by (market, timestamp_received, event_seq) where event_seq is a within-file sequence number for tie-breaking.

2. Drop exact duplicate events (same market, timestamp, sequence, payload).

3. Drop events with malformed numeric fields (rare; logged at WARNING level).

4. For book events with empty bids and asks, treat as market dormancy markers, not as data quality failures.

The percentage of events dropped under each cleaning rule is reported per file in the production G5 output JSON.

B.8 Diagnostic chronological-prefix subsamples The originally pre-registered analysis-sample selection rule (plan v1.2 §5.4) was: “rank distinct markets by min(first_event_timestamp) and take the first N ”. We ran this rule at three subsample sizes for the gate evaluation before the day-1 selection-bias finding led us to replace it (Section 5.5). The full per-class breakdowns are recorded here for reference. The three diagnostic runs are retained in the record as the empirical basis for the day- 1 selection-bias finding documented in Section 5.5. The qualitative finding (chronological prefix samples within-day, not within-week) is stable across all three runs; the quantitative trajectory (sports share 66.6% → 74.6% → 89.3%, resolution ceiling 34.6% → 27.3% → 30.9%) characterizes the strength of the selection bias.

C.1 Parameter discipline Every framework parameter is classified into exactly one of two categories.

Data-estimated. Parameter is computed from the observable data stream (the PMXT v2 archive plus the metadata and resolution joins). The estimator is specified below; the estimator is fixed by this appendix and may not be tuned to improve empirical results.

C.2 Estimators for data-estimated parameters Realized volatility σ̂t . Windowed realized volatility of the index It over the trailing Wσ hours, computed from log-return increments at the natural CLOB event spacing. Estimator: 1 X 2 σ̂t2 = log It [s] − log It [s− ] |Tt | s∈T t

where Tt is the set of all index updates in the window [t − Wσ , t) and s− is the immediately preceding update. Window: Wσ = 1 hour. Boundary handling: when It ≤ Itfloor = 0.005 or It ≥ 1−Itfloor , log-return computation is replaced with the linear-return increment (It [s]−It [s− ]) to avoid the singularity in log p at the boundary; σ̂t continues to be reported in the same units. The boundary treatment is documented as part of the estimator; it is not adjustable.

Terminal-jump probability π̂tjump . Estimator of the probability of a terminal jump within the current margin horizon HM , conditional on observable signals. Defined as

π̂tjump = f (T − t), It , Nt 

where (T − t) is the time to scheduled resolution, It is the current index level, and Nt is a vector of indicators for upcoming scheduled-news events within [t, t + HM ] assembled from the news-window labels (see Section 5.1). The functional form f is the empirical hazard estimator computed on the training window 2026-04-21T00 to 2026-04-24T23 UTC (the first four days of the empirical week); the test window for E1, E2, E3 is 2026-04-25T00 to 2026-04-27T23 UTC (the remaining three days), plus markets with first event before the train cutoff but resolution in the test window. The chronological train-then-test split is locked here; it is not re-shuffled to improve fit. Margin horizon: HM = 1 hour.

Effective depth Dt . Aggregate displayed depth within ∆depth = 200 basis points of the prevailing mid-price, summed across both sides of the order book at time t. Estimator: Dt = qt (p) X

where qt (p) is the displayed quantity at price level p at time t. Computed at every book event from the reconstructed order book; carried forward to subsequent price_change events until the next full book snapshot.

Manipulation cost proxy κt . Notional cost to move the index It by a specified target ∆manip under a one-shot market-order execution model against the displayed order book at time t. Computed by simulating a single market order of increasing size against the order book until the executed price crosses It + ∆manip . Target: ∆manip = 0.05 (i.e., cost to move the index by 5 percentage points under the one-shot model). Interpretation. κt is an instantaneous displayed-depth measure under a specific (oneshot) execution model. It is not a universal lower bound on the cost of all manipulation strategies: strategic order splitting, inter-event liquidity replenishment, or coordinated multivenue execution may reduce the realized cost of a price-impact attack relative to what the one-shot computation reports; conversely, time-pressured attackers facing detection or countertrading risk may pay strictly more. We use κt as a conservative, deterministic book-thinness proxy for the comparative analyses of Section 8, not as a definitive manipulation-cost estimate. Where the interpretation matters for a specific empirical claim, we say so explicitly in the text.

C.4 Falsifiability thresholds for E1, E2, E3 The falsifiability discipline of Section 5 requires that the paper’s main empirical claims have explicit failure conditions stated in advance. The thresholds below are the conditions under which each experiment’s central claim is treated as falsified.

Framing: materiality, not safety. The thresholds below are not claimed to be universal safety standards or deployment criteria. They are materiality thresholds: below them, the proposed framework does not improve enough over the naive baseline to justify its added complexity. A framework that requires substantial additional engineering (composite robust index, jump-aware tiered margin, anti-cascade dampening, resolution-zone protocol) must clear a non-trivial materiality bar to be worth specifying; otherwise, a simpler design dominates. The numerical levels are policy choices calibrated against the sense of “meaningful improvement that justifies non-trivial engineering complexity”, not against any external regulatory or safety floor.

E1 (stylized facts). The framework’s design assumptions about the bounded-event process (boundary depth asymmetry, terminal jump distribution, basis behavior under information arrival) must be empirically present in the analysis sample at materially significant levels. Specifically:

• Depth asymmetry, ρ: The ratio of within-book depth on the long side versus the short side of the prevailing mid-price, in the boundary region It < δ, must be at least ρfloor = 1.5 at the median market in the analysis sample. Rationale: ρ < 1.5 means the depth asymmetry that Assumption 3 of Section 3.1 requires is not materially present; without it, Proposition 2 (which depends on Assumption 3) does not have an empirical anchor and must be qualified.

• Terminal jump magnitude, evaluated by class: Markets that resolve within the empirical window must exhibit terminal-jump magnitudes (the change in It in the final hour before resolution) consistent with the bounded-event model. Specifically: the median absolute terminal jump |∆It [τ − , τ ]| must be at least 0.10 (10 percentage points) at the median resolved market evaluated both pooled and per event class. If the pooled sample fails the floor but one or more event classes pass it individually, the framework’s jump-aware margin claim is retained for the passing classes and explicitly qualified for the failing classes. This per-class evaluation guards against a quiet single week falsifying the framework on classes where it would otherwise apply. Rationale for 0.10: a terminal jump under 10 percentage points means the boundary collapse dynamic that the jump-aware margin schedule in Definition 4 is designed to handle is not the binding empirical phenomenon; below this, the schedule is over-engineered for the data.

E2 (counterfactual replay). The resolution-aware framework configuration C2 must outperform the naive crypto-perp port C0 on both trader-independent metrics on observed paths. Specifically:

• Liquidation rate (E2a, trader-independent): The rate at which forced liquidations occur on observed paths under C2 must be lower than under C0 by at least 30% (relative reduction). Rationale: 30% is the minimum material improvement floor; below this, the additional engineering of leverage compression and jump-aware margin does not earn its complexity over a static-margin baseline.

• Insurance fund drawdown (E2b, trader-independent): The total notional drawdown to a hypothetical engine-funded insurance pool under C2 must be lower than under C0

by at least 50%. Rationale: a risk-engine claim about capital protection should at least halve aggregate capital stress relative to the baseline; below 50%, the framework’s capital-protection contribution is too modest to support the framing of the paper’s central design claim.

• Synthetic robustness layer (E2c): For the synthetic trader-population layer, the framework’s improvement over C0 should be robust across the documented parameter ranges in Section E. E2c is robustness, not primary; a failure at this layer triggers a discussionof-bounds section, not falsification of the central claim.

E3 (resolution-zone protocol). The resolution-zone protocol M3 (multi-stage with leverage compression and boundary-funding correction) must produce qualitatively different behavior than M0 (no resolution-zone protocol) in the final hour before resolution. Specifically:

• Final-hour liquidation reduction: The fraction of positions liquidated in the final hour must be reduced by at least 50% under M3 versus M0 . Rationale: the resolution-zone protocol’s primary purpose is to protect positions from the terminal-collapse dynamic; halving the final-hour liquidation rate is the minimum threshold at which the protocol is contributing materially.

• Bad-debt reduction: The frequency of bad-debt events (liquidations where the insurance pool absorbs uncovered loss) must be reduced by at least 75% under M3 versus M0 . Rationale: bad debt is the tail-risk target of the framework; the threshold is intentionally more demanding than the others because tail-risk reduction is what justifies the engineering complexity of the resolution-zone protocol over simpler alternatives. A reduction below 75% means the protocol does not adequately address its principal design purpose.

C.5 Honest reporting of negative results If E1, E2, or E3 falsifies a central claim per the thresholds above, the relevant claim in Section 1.4 (the contributions list) is qualified or withdrawn, and Sections 8 and 11 report the failure explicitly with analysis of why. Reviewer 2’s guidance on r1.5.2 framed this commitment directly: the paper is valuable even when the framework fails on some dimensions, provided the failure is documented honestly. We commit to that here as a locked rule, not an aspiration.

D.6 Run-loop infrastructure: stop conditions and queue ordering Runs that process market data in long-running stages (metadata_join, resolution_join) check stop conditions periodically inside the stage — after every N = 100 markets processed or every T = 60 seconds, whichever comes first — rather than only at stage boundaries. The check inspects:

• Peak resident memory (default threshold 14 GB).

• Wall time since run start (configurable; the present runs used 5 hours for chronological subsamples, 18 hours for the stratified analysis sample run).

• Rolling Gamma 404 rate over the last 1000 markets (default threshold 5%).

• Rolling UMA hit rate over the last 1000 markets (default floor 90%; can be lowered with –uma-hit-stop flag for runs where partial UMA coverage is acceptable).

• Presence of an external STOP file in the working directory.

The two rate-based conditions (Gamma 404 rate, UMA hit rate) require at least 100 samples in the rolling window before the corresponding threshold can fire, to avoid false positives at the start of a run where rolling rates are noisy. The remaining three conditions (RSS, wall time, external STOP file) fire immediately whenever the threshold is crossed. On trigger, the run saves a partial-state JSON evaluation/output/<run_id>_partial_state.json containing the run identifier, the condition that fired and its measured value, markets processed so far, and rolling statistics, then exits with the corresponding exit code. The cache state at the time of trigger is preserved on disk; a re-run with the same parameters will resume from cache, processing only markets not yet completed.

Queue ordering for stratified samples. The stratified-by-day analysis sample selection (Section 5.5) submits markets to the executor in round-robin-by-day order: the k-th submitted market rotates through the seven days of the empirical window. The CLI flag –queue-order accepts round-robin (default) or sequential. Round-robin ordering ensures that partial state at any moment during the run is a representative cross-day sample, so a run interrupted by a stop condition produces an analyzable (if not complete) partial sample rather than a day-1-skewed prefix. Historical note: the CC-003.11 stratified analysis-sample run and the CC-004 stylized-facts compute used interleave=False (sequential) ordering, predating the round-robin default of CC-005 onward. The set of markets sampled is deterministic in either ordering (same locked seed produces same markets); only submission order differs. Sequential-ordering output is not corrupted by the ordering choice, only its partial-state-while-running representativeness is. Replications of those runs with current code (–queue-order round-robin) will produce the same numerical outputs.

Persistent HTTP connections. Both ingest/market_metadata.py (Gamma) and ingest/uma_resolutio (UMA) use a thread-local httpx.Client per worker, persistent across calls. This removes the per-call TCP handshake and TLS negotiation overhead that an earlier version of the code incurred, where a fresh client was instantiated per market. The resulting throughput improvement is observable in any API-bound stage. Throughput benchmarking versus the earlier per-call client pattern was deferred from CC-005 to the first live API run after the fix (docs/cc005_t21_t22_report.md §4.5), so the architectural fix is in place but the empirical magnitude of the improvement is characterized in the run logs of subsequent runs rather than in isolation.
